title: Check if an array is sorted (compare adjacent elements).
shortTitle: Check if an Array Is Sorted
keyPoints: Compare each element with its next neighbour; if any earlier element is greater than the next, the array is not sorted.
Fail fast by returning false at the first violation, saving work when the error is near the front.
Empty and single-element arrays are trivially sorted because there are no adjacent pairs to violate.
Decide deliberately between strict ascending (no duplicates) and non-strict ascending (duplicates allowed).
Accept a Comparator parameter to make the method reusable for ascending, descending, or custom orders.
Time is O(n) in the worst case (fully sorted) and O(1) space.

s1_definition.oneliner: Walk adjacent pairs; if any earlier element is greater than the next, it is not sorted; otherwise it is.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Adjacent comparison** – check each element against its immediate neighbour.
- **Fail fast** – return `false` at the first violation to avoid unnecessary work.
- **Trivially sorted** – empty and single-element arrays pass because there are no pairs to violate.
- **Ordering policy** – `<=` allows duplicates (non-strict); `<` requires strictly increasing.
- **O(n) time, O(1) space** – one pass through the array with no extra data structures.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India produces a daily settlement file where transactions must already be ordered by timestamp. A clerk walks down the rows comparing each row's time with the next. The instant a later row has an earlier time, the file is flagged as out of order. If every pair is in order all the way down, the file passes.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Checking whether an array is sorted is a single pass over adjacent pairs. For ascending order I compare each element with the next and return false the moment I find a violation. If the scan completes, the array is sorted. It is linear time, constant space, and fails fast.

Empty and single-element arrays are trivially sorted. I decide strict versus non-strict ordering deliberately: non-strict allows equal neighbours, which is right when duplicates are legitimate, while strict enforces uniqueness.

To make it reusable I accept a Comparator so the same loop checks ascending, descending, or any custom order. Fail-fast matters in practice: on a large settlement file that is corrupt near the top, returning at the first violation avoids scanning millions of remaining rows.

In my banking project at National Bank of India I used this as a gate in the settlement ingestion pipeline, because the downstream reconciliation engine assumes sorted input.

Remember one sentence: compare adjacent pairs and return false at the first violation, return true only if every pair passes.
